title: How Cult Deprogramming Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain cult deprogramming in the United States in the 1970s and 1980s. They trace the anti-cult climate that followed the Manson family and Jonestown, and the rise of Ted Patrick and the Cult Awareness Network, which used kidnapping and forced "deprogramming" to pull adults and young people out of groups. They cover how conservatorship laws, parental consent, and the age of majority made the practice quasi-legal, and describe notable cases including Stephanie Rthymiller's abduction and rape in Ohio, and Jason Scott's case in Washington State. They also cover the Scientology-backed lawsuit that bankrupted the Cult Awareness Network, which was then bought by Scientology, and Rick Ross's later move into voluntary exit counseling. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about hot air balloon ground crews in Napa Valley.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about the value of the minute before recording and introduce the topic of cult deprogramming as a dark chapter in American history fueled by fear.

segments.title: Generational divide and new religious movements
segments.summary: The hosts describe the late 1960s and 1970s generation gap and the rise of groups then called cults, most of them Bible-based Christian or Eastern-influenced, which are now called new religious movements. They note the charismatic central figure common to these groups.

segments.title: Jonestown and the origins of Ted Patrick
segments.summary: After the Manson family and Jonestown showed cults could be destructive, parents grew desperate. Ted Patrick, a former high school dropout raised in Chattanooga, infiltrated the Children of God after being approached about his son and nephew, and began offering deprogramming for a fee.

segments.title: Legal loopholes: age of majority and conservatorship
segments.summary: Patrick believed parents hiring him would shield him from kidnapping charges. The age of majority of twenty-one meant children were still minors in many cases, and adults could be placed under conservatorship on loose evidence, often backed by a psychologist's statement, allowing parents to transfer power to deprogrammers.

segments.title: Cult Awareness Network and early tactics
segments.summary: Patrick initially hired street thugs for abductions and later worked with Sandra Sachs and a henchman called Goose. Cases included a woman who left the Greek Orthodox Church and an English professor, Sarah Worth, whose activism her mother opposed. The hosts describe how the public and courts widely accepted the anti-cult view, and how Patrick was jailed only twice.
topics: media and public opinion on cults

segments.title: Stephanie Rthymiller case and deprogramming methods
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1970s abduction of Stephanie Rthymiller in Ohio, who was taken and raped over seven days by a Patrick henchman because her parents believed she was a lesbian, and the judge's comments at trial. They then describe the methods: sleep and food deprivation, berating, and physical abuse, with the goal of forcing a 'snap' and a claimed conversion, which families cited as proof it worked.

segments.title: Jason Scott case and Scientology lawsuit
segments.summary: Jason Scott was kidnapped in Washington State, held and abused for days, then faked a change of heart and escaped to police at a restaurant. A civil suit backed by Scientology lawyers bankrupted the Cult Awareness Network, which Scientology later bought and renamed. Scott later sold his settlement to Rick Ross for much less than the amount awarded.

segments.title: Exit counseling and moral complexity
segments.summary: Rick Ross now does exit counseling, a voluntary family-based intervention, and the hosts reflect on the moral murkiness, since some former deprogrammees say the practice helped them. They also note the 1980s Satanic panic and mention a planned future episode.

segments.title: Listener mail: hot air balloons
segments.summary: Ryan from Washington, D.C. describes his time on a Napa Valley hot air balloon ground crew, including an emergency landing in a wheat field and a champagne apology to the landowner.
